title: The Iran Deal Draft Is Out. Here Is What Is in It — and What India Stands to Gain.
excerpt: Iran has reportedly agreed to abandon its nuclear weapons programme. The US will release roughly $20 billion in frozen assets and waive oil sanctions. The Strait of Hormuz — which carried 40 per cent of India's crude imports — would reopen immediately.
body:
The broad contours of a US-Iran peace deal are now visible for the first time — and if the agreement holds, it would end the most disruptive geopolitical shock to hit India's economy in years. For the Indian diaspora across the US, UK, and Canada, the resolution of this crisis carries significant implications, from the stability of family finances back home to the cost of travel and investment prospects in India.

According to an Iranian official briefed on the draft, Iran has agreed to abandon its nuclear weapons programme as part of an initial memorandum of understanding brokered by Pakistan. The promise, described as part of a phased framework, covers a commitment not to "obtain or produce a nuclear weapon" through any means. Further discussions on what to do with Iran's existing enriched uranium stockpile will take place over the next two months as part of a finalised agreement.

The draft also includes the release of nearly $20 billion in frozen Iranian assets held abroad and the lifting of US sanctions on Iranian oil exports. In return, Iran would immediately lift its blockade of the Strait of Hormuz — the chokepoint through which roughly 20 per cent of the world's oil and LNG passes, and which has been effectively closed to most commercial traffic since the war began on February 28.

## The Signing — Maybe Today, Maybe Not

US President Donald Trump said on Saturday that the deal was "scheduled to get signed tomorrow" — meaning Sunday, June 15 — and that the Strait would be "open to all" immediately after signing. Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif confirmed that Islamabad was preparing for an electronic signing, with technical-level talks to follow next week.

But Iran pushed back on the timeline. Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei said the signing "will not be tomorrow," while cautioning that "the possibility of this happening in the coming days cannot be ruled out." Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi described the document as the "Islamabad memorandum of understanding" and called on media to "refrain from entering speculation about its content."

US Vice President JD Vance intervened to control the narrative, posting that "the Iranians are not receiving any cash" simply for signing. He described the deal as "structured to ensure that the US and its allies' concerns are prioritised" and said economic benefits would flow to Iran only if it "meets its obligations."

Last-minute disputes over the language on ceasing hostilities in Lebanon remain unresolved, according to Reuters. The draft reportedly does not include restrictions on Iran's ballistic missiles.

## What This Means for India

India's exposure to the Hormuz crisis has been severe. The Strait carried roughly 40 per cent of the country's crude imports before the war. Since the closure, India's oil-and-gas import bill jumped 53 per cent in a single month, Brent crude surged to nearly $120 a barrel, and
